name: Eleme
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Bond, Oliver. 2006. Aspects of Eleme verbal morphosyntax. PhD thesis, University of Manchester. 324 pp. (open PDF, author's site:https://oliverbond.info/Bond-2006.pdf)
catalog_quote: [p.53, 3.1] Eleme is a tonal language with a rich phonological system. [p.66, 3.5 Tone] While the majority of Niger-Congo languages are thought to be tonal (Williamson 1989a:26), all Cross River languages, including the Ogonoid languages, exhibit contrastive tone systems (Faraclas 1989:388). There are three contrastive level tones in Eleme, a high tone (H) marked as [acute; diacritic garbled in], a low tone (L) marked as [grave], and a mid tone (M), which remains unmarked. Tone is employed both lexically (3.5.1) and grammatically (3.5.2) in the language. [p.288, 7.5] This indicates that the presence of distinctive tone is not a suitable criteria for distinguishing phonologically free units from phonologically bound ones in Eleme. The stress system of Eleme remains to be studied and therefore additional evidence from this domain will not be discussed here.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Eleme has three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) with lexical and grammatical function; the best available first-hand description gives no word-stress rule and states explicitly that Eleme stress has not been studied.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only incidental remarks that word-initial noun prefixes are 'unstressed' and prone to aphaeresis after a verb (p.72), which is not a placement rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at word level (lexical minimal pairs, verb tone classes, grammatical tone on prefixes/clitics); vowel harmony is word-bounded and used to delimit prosodic words (p.66). No statement about phrase-level prominence or citation-form stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bond 2006 describes Eleme as a whole (glottocode elem1253, ISO elm); speakers of both dialects, Nchia (socially dominant, the variety of all previous studies) and Odido, were consulted, differences said to be mainly lexical (p.~20). Ngulube's papers do not name a dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Bond, Oliver. 2016. Negation through reduplication and tone: implications for the Lexical Functional Grammar/Paradigm Function Morphology interface. Journal of Linguistics 52(2): 277-310. (published online 24 July 2015)
tone_statements.quote: Examples are presented in a phonemic orthography consistent with the IPA, with the exception of <r> used for [ɹ] and <y> used for [j]. Eleme has three tones: high (marked with an acute accent), mid (unmarked) and low (marked with a grave accent). ... their polarity and aspect values are indicated by a tonal pattern across the stem that distinguishes them from other segmentally identical verb forms. ... The HL tone pattern on the reduplicated stem in (6a) distinguishes the Negative Habitual form from the Future verb form in (6b) which has a HH pattern
tone_statements.locator: note 2 (endnotes) (three tones); sec. 2.2 'Negative Habituals' (HL vs HH stem patterns); accepted-manuscript pagination (publisher pp. 277-310 not in this copy)
tone_statements.summary: Three tones, high, mid and low (mid unmarked); verbs fall into lexical tone classes, and Negative Habitual vs Future are distinguished only by HL vs HH tone patterns on the reduplicated stem.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Phonological properties of the verb' (pp. 53-78): 'Eleme is a tonal language' (p.53); three contrastive level tones H, M, L, used lexically and grammatically (sec. 3.5, p.66); tone classes of verbs, tone in reduplication, tone stability under elision. No stress rule anywhere; p.288 (sec. 7.5) states explicitly 'The stress system of Eleme remains to be studied'. Only incidental uses of 'unstressed' (noun prefixes prone to aphaeresis, p.72; pronoun typology p.~88).

sources.citation: Ngulube, Isaac Eyi. 2014. Syllabification, tone marking, and minimality in Eleme. African Research Review (AFRREV) 8(4), S/No 35: 1-17. doi:10.4314/afrrev.v8i4.1
sources.note: No statement about word stress as such. Presents a 'tone marking' algorithm in Halle & Vergnaud's (1987) stress framework: 'place a low tone on the first syllable within the (grammatical) word' (p.2); 'tone mark every other vowel.. from left to right', binary left-headed feet, word-initial vowels and word-final /i/ extraprosodic, minimal word = binary foot (pp.10-11, 15).
